questions.question: Which statement best captures the difference between unconstrained optimization and optimization with orthogonality constraints on matrix variables?
questions.choice_A: Unconstrained optimization searches over all of $\mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, while orthogonality-constrained optimization restricts search to a curved subset (a manifold) where columns are orthonormal.
questions.choice_B: Unconstrained optimization always converges faster than constrained optimization because there are no constraints to enforce.
questions.choice_C: Orthogonality constraints convert every optimization problem into a convex program over a polytope.
questions.choice_D: Orthogonality constraints remove the need for gradients because feasibility implies optimality.

questions.question: What is the Stiefel manifold $\mathrm{St}(n,p)$?
questions.choice_A: The set of all $n \times n$ orthogonal matrices with determinant $+1$.
questions.choice_B: The set of all $n \times p$ real matrices whose columns are orthonormal, i.e., $X^\top X = I_p$.
questions.choice_C: The set of all $p \times p$ positive definite matrices embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$.
questions.choice_D: The set of all $n \times p$ matrices with orthogonal rows.

questions.question: In manifold optimization, what is a retraction?
questions.choice_A: A function that exactly follows the geodesic defined by the exponential map.
questions.choice_B: A projection onto the manifold that is globally optimal in the least-squares sense.
questions.choice_C: A smooth map from the tangent space to the manifold that locally approximates the exponential map and preserves first-order information.
questions.choice_D: A numerical routine for computing step sizes in line search.

questions.question: Why is the exponential map often avoided in practical algorithms on the Stiefel manifold?
questions.choice_A: It is non-differentiable at most points.
questions.choice_B: It does not preserve orthogonality when implemented in finite precision.
questions.choice_C: It lacks a closed form on Lie groups.
questions.choice_D: It can be computationally expensive due to matrix exponentials of skew-symmetric blocks, whereas cheaper retractions (QR, polar, Cayley) often suffice.

questions.question: Which update scheme enforces orthogonality by projecting a tentative Euclidean step back onto the Stiefel manifold?
questions.choice_A: Projected gradient descent using a retraction (e.g., via QR or polar decomposition).
questions.choice_B: Standard Euclidean gradient descent without modification.
questions.choice_C: Newton's method with no constraints.
questions.choice_D: Stochastic gradient descent with momentum in $\mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$.

questions.question: What is the Riemannian gradient on the Stiefel manifold in relation to the Euclidean gradient?
questions.choice_A: It is the same as the Euclidean gradient because the manifold is embedded in Euclidean space.
questions.choice_B: It is the orthogonal projection of the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space at the current point.
questions.choice_C: It is the Hessian-vector product applied to the Euclidean gradient.
questions.choice_D: It is obtained by normalizing the Euclidean gradient to unit Frobenius norm.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the tangent space $T_X \mathrm{St}(n,p)$ at $X$?
questions.choice_A: All matrices $\Delta$ such that $X \Delta^\top + \Delta X^\top = 0$.
questions.choice_B: All matrices $\Delta$ such that $\Delta^\top \Delta = 0$.
questions.choice_C: All matrices $\Delta$ such that $X^\top \Delta + \Delta^\top X = 0$.
questions.choice_D: All matrices $\Delta$ such that $\Delta X = X \Delta$.

questions.question: What is a key difference between QR- and polar-decomposition-based retractions for enforcing orthogonality?
questions.choice_A: QR ensures exact orthogonality while polar only approximates it to first order.
questions.choice_B: Polar retractions minimize distance to the tentative step in the Frobenius norm, while QR retractions do not have this optimality property.
questions.choice_C: QR is differentiable everywhere, while polar is not differentiable anywhere.
questions.choice_D: Polar retractions typically require an SVD or matrix square root, often more expensive but better conditioned, whereas QR is cheaper but may be less stable when $R$ has small diagonals.

questions.question: Which statement about the Cayley transform in orthogonality-constrained optimization is correct?
questions.choice_A: It maps any matrix to an orthogonal matrix by $Q = (I - A)(I + A)^{-1}$ for arbitrary $A$.
questions.choice_B: When $A$ is skew-symmetric, the Cayley transform yields an orthogonal matrix and defines a cheap update that approximates the exponential map.
questions.choice_C: It requires computing a full SVD at each step.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees global convergence irrespective of step size.

questions.question: In projected gradient descent on the Stiefel manifold, why is projecting the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space beneficial before retraction?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the need for retractions entirely.
questions.choice_B: It yields a feasible descent direction that respects the manifold's geometry and avoids leaving the manifold to first order.
questions.choice_C: It ensures the step size is always optimal.
questions.choice_D: It converts the problem into an unconstrained one on a linear subspace.

questions.question: What is a practical challenge when differentiating through QR-based orthogonalization in deep learning models?
questions.choice_A: The QR decomposition is not available on GPUs.
questions.choice_B: QR cannot maintain orthogonality under backpropagation.
questions.choice_C: Non-uniqueness due to sign/ordering conventions can introduce discontinuities; careful handling (e.g., fixing signs or using continuous variants) is needed for stable gradients.
questions.choice_D: Automatic differentiation frameworks do not support any factorization routines.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid retraction on the Stiefel manifold?
questions.choice_A: Adding the gradient directly and re-normalizing each column independently.
questions.choice_B: Projecting onto the manifold by solving a semidefinite program.
questions.choice_C: Taking a step along the Euclidean gradient and then orthogonalizing with exact Gram–Schmidt, which is first-order equivalent to the exponential map.
questions.choice_D: Performing QR or polar decomposition of $X + \eta$ where $\eta$ is a tangent step, and returning the orthogonal factor.

questions.question: When comparing Gram–Schmidt, Householder QR, and polar decomposition for orthogonalization inside optimization loops, which trade-off is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Classical Gram–Schmidt is cheapest but least stable; Householder QR is more stable but costlier; polar is often most accurate but can be the most expensive.
questions.choice_B: All three have identical numerical stability and computational cost.
questions.choice_C: Polar is always cheaper than QR because it avoids matrix factorizations.
questions.choice_D: Householder QR is unstable unless combined with reorthogonalization.

questions.question: Which statement best describes geodesics on the orthogonal group $\mathrm{O}(n)$?
questions.choice_A: They are solutions to linear ODEs with symmetric generators.
questions.choice_B: They are curves of the form $Q(t) = Q_0 \exp(t\,\Omega)$ with $\Omega$ skew-symmetric, under the canonical metric.
questions.choice_C: They are straight lines in matrix space, $Q(t) = Q_0 + t\Omega$, that remain orthogonal.
questions.choice_D: They are not defined because $\mathrm{O}(n)$ is not a manifold.

questions.question: Why might one prefer Riemannian optimization over simple projected Euclidean methods for orthogonality constraints?
questions.choice_A: Riemannian methods avoid computing gradients altogether.
questions.choice_B: They operate with intrinsic notions of gradient and Hessian on the manifold, often improving convergence and reducing bias from repeated projections.
questions.choice_C: They guarantee global optimality for nonconvex problems.
questions.choice_D: They eliminate the need to choose step sizes.

questions.question: In the context of the Procrustes problem, what role does the polar decomposition play?
questions.choice_A: It provides the orthogonal factor closest (in Frobenius norm) to a given matrix, solving the orthogonal Procrustes projection.
questions.choice_B: It factors a matrix into an orthogonal and a lower-triangular component.
questions.choice_C: It yields the minimum-norm solution to an underdetermined linear system.
questions.choice_D: It computes geodesics on the Stiefel manifold exactly.

questions.question: What is a common way to parameterize local updates on the Stiefel manifold that preserves orthogonality to first order?
questions.choice_A: Update $X \leftarrow X + \alpha G$ for Euclidean gradient $G$ without any modification.
questions.choice_B: Update $X \leftarrow (I + \tfrac{\alpha}{2}A)^{-1}(I - \tfrac{\alpha}{2}A)X$ with $A$ skew-symmetric (Cayley-like update).
questions.choice_C: Update $X \leftarrow X + \alpha X$.
questions.choice_D: Update $X \leftarrow X + \alpha I$.

questions.question: What is vector transport in Riemannian optimization, and why is it needed?
questions.choice_A: It is a method to compute step sizes; it is needed to guarantee descent.
questions.choice_B: It moves tangent vectors from one tangent space to another along a curve, needed to define momentum/second-order methods consistently on manifolds.
questions.choice_C: It projects any matrix onto the manifold; it is needed to enforce feasibility.
questions.choice_D: It computes the exponential map; it is needed to follow geodesics exactly.

questions.question: Which consideration is most relevant when choosing between exact orthogonalization (e.g., polar) and approximate methods (e.g., one-step Gram–Schmidt) inside each optimization iteration?
questions.choice_A: Exact methods always accelerate convergence regardless of cost.
questions.choice_B: Approximate methods typically reduce per-iteration cost, but can accumulate feasibility errors or induce drift, potentially harming convergence accuracy.
questions.choice_C: Approximate methods are always more numerically stable.
questions.choice_D: Exact methods cannot be differentiated through.

questions.question: How does the choice of metric on the Stiefel manifold affect optimization algorithms?
questions.choice_A: It does not affect algorithms, as all metrics are equivalent in practice.
questions.choice_B: Different metrics change the Riemannian gradient, Hessian, and step geometry, influencing convergence behavior and computational cost.
questions.choice_C: Metrics only affect the line search, not the update direction.
questions.choice_D: Metrics determine whether the manifold is smooth.

questions.question: Which practical issue arises when differentiating through SVD/polar-based projections to enforce orthogonality?
questions.choice_A: These decompositions are linear maps, so backpropagation is trivial.
questions.choice_B: They can be ill-conditioned or non-differentiable when singular values are clustered or repeated, requiring regularization or careful implementation for stable gradients.
questions.choice_C: The polar decomposition cannot be computed in finite precision.
questions.choice_D: Backpropagation through SVD is unsupported in modern autodiff libraries.

questions.question: For large-scale problems on $\mathrm{St}(n,p)$ with $n \gg p$, which strategy often offers a good computational trade-off per iteration?
questions.choice_A: Using the exact exponential map via a full $n \times n$ matrix exponential at each step.
questions.choice_B: Projecting the Euclidean gradient onto the tangent space and using a QR-based retraction, leveraging thin QR to keep cost $\mathcal{O}(np^2)$.
questions.choice_C: Computing a full SVD-based polar retraction on an $n \times n$ embedding each iteration.
questions.choice_D: Avoiding retractions and letting feasibility drift, to minimize computation.
